The beginning and end of circular motion are not points. They are positions, and the two positions are never the same at the same time.

The beginning and end may be found in different, non-overlapping parts of motion. There are also possible beginnings and ends that can coincide because they are relative to what comes before or after. Along with an actual beginning and end, these make three kinds.
This change follows the underlying thing; it is not merely something that happens to it by accident.

“In” here means “within time.” Time is one of the six things on which motion depends. If there were motion in the category of “when,” there would have to be another time in which that motion occurred.

Motion occurring within motion would only slow the first movement. In the same way, if there were motion in the category of “when,” it would slow the passage of time. There is no impossibility in that unless it leads to an endless series. When all the categories change along with a changing substance, they do not change merely in name. Each has a change suited to it and a corresponding time, so that none falls behind the substance it belongs to or runs ahead of it. Think of someone aboard a ship, who moves with the ship while also being able to move about or sit still on board.

Neither of Avicenna's arguments settles the question. First, motion in the category of “when” would be a different individual motion from the motion through which the body comes to have a time. Nothing has shown that this is impossible. Second, another “when” would only make the substance more deeply involved in the first time, slowing its passage. There is no difficulty unless this leads to an endless regress.

Sadra reads Avicenna's words this way because “when”—existing in time—belongs to motion and to what moves. The movement and its time extend continuously together. A change from one month, hour, or minute to the next therefore proceeds gradually: there is no actual break in either time or what exists in it. Sadra takes Avicenna to be referring to the point already established: although a process unfolds gradually, the existence of that process considered as a process does not itself unfold in stages.

I have another reading. Avicenna says “transition,” not “motion.” He may be speaking of passing from one kind of time to another, as from night to day, or from one particular hour to the next. That transition happens at the instant that separates them. Though time has no actual gap, its different kinds and individual stretches have a boundary; without that boundary, we could not distinguish them.

Avicenna means that a thing's time depends on its motion. Time is the setting in which motion occurs, and so it exists whenever the motion exists. To say that motion is “in” time does not mean that time is its subject, as a path is the subject of motion; it means that time provides the setting for motion.

This would mean that motion in the categories of acting and being acted upon is the same motion viewed from two sides: as motion of the mover and as motion of the moved thing. The question remains which category motion itself belongs to. Sadra treats it as a way that existence appears in the world of nature.

The change could also be from weak heating to stronger heating. If someone objects that change in quality passes through several shades, we reply that a quality is a stable state that can exist at an instant; it need not remain unchanged in the next instant. There need not be a pause between its degrees. Acting and being acted upon, by contrast, are gradual processes and cannot be complete in a single instant. A pause between them is no more surprising than a pause between two opposite motions.

This argument can be challenged. If a category exists only together with motion, then it must have instantaneous limits or instances where motion ends. These would be possible even if they are always potential. Just as an extended quantity can be divided again after an earlier division, a number can be divided into units that themselves contain tens. So the instant that is a boundary for one motion can be part of a time for another motion. The instant need not become time for the motion it bounds.
The more natural reading reverses this point, unless the text is deliberately reversing it or means the instant on the assumption that motion occurs within it.

All features change along with nature, but not all have the same kind of change. For some, change is part of their existence, as with the categories in which motion occurs. For others, such as acting, being acted upon, time, and motion, change belongs to the idea of the category. For still others, such as relation, change belongs indirectly to the thing from which the relation is drawn.
This reply would work only if motion had first been defined, and then used as the standard for defining rest. Why not define rest first and motion from it?

Time measures motion; the instant is a boundary of time, and before and after are temporal relations. Motion can be defined without using rest: its first completion and its gradual passage from potentiality to actuality are enough. Even if rest were defined first, motion could then be defined from it.
The note simply says that this point is disputed.
The change comes from within the body in the relevant place. So it does not follow that the change occurs without a cause.

At every instant, the moving thing is described as moving through the whole stretch of time, though its motion is not contained in one instant. What depends on a thing in its own realm cannot be separated from what it depends on in a higher realm. For example, time-bound existence depends on timeless existence, and the existence of the heavens depends on the universal intellect.

If a body's motion stops and later resumes, the new motion is not the same individual motion as before, because a different time has passed. The personal continuity that made it one motion was broken. If continuity is not broken, what occurs later is still part of the same individual motion.

The wording falls short. For a motion to remain one individual motion, five things must remain the same: its subject, time, path, starting point, and destination. Changing either endpoint changes the individual motion even when the others stay the same, just as changing the path does.

You may object that a change of starting point or destination makes motions different in kind, as the author will say below. But a change of path can do so too. Moreover, an individual motion belongs to a kind, and that kind depends on what makes it the kind it is. A change that produces a different kind must also produce a different individual motion.

Changing the mover alone need not produce a new motion. Two people may keep the same wheel turning, or two sources of heat may warm the same water, provided its continuous change is not interrupted. This does not mean that two independent causes each produce the very same effect. In short, the loss of any one of those five things ends the motion's individual unity, and a difference in any of them makes it another motion.

The motion's defining principles are like the essential features that make a thing a particular kind. These are its starting point, the kind of change, and its destination—not its agent, its subject, or its time. A change in kind in one of these principles gives a different kind of motion; a merely individual difference gives a different individual motion. The path can distinguish a kind as well as an individual, so there is no contradiction in mentioning it in both ways.
Speed and slowness do not even make motions different individuals, much less different kinds. The same motion becomes faster as it nears its goal.

This is a concession to the objection. In fact, motion is more unified than a straight line, which is one continuous quantity. If even ten, whose nature is to be many, has a unity and identity of its own, then motion must have them all the more, since its many parts are only potential.

This supports the earlier reply. Everything in the world combines what has passed with what is still to come, what is fading with what is renewed, and parts with a single identity. In this way, it remains one whole.

A shadow or patch of light on flowing water may look like one thing, though it is renewed at every instant. This is like the continual renewal of the world: one world passes away and another comes to be, through God's names as the One who takes away and the One who brings forth. This is the way of God, and it does not change. The world, viewed in itself, is always being renewed; viewed in relation to God, the Eternal, it is one and unchanging.

This completes the answer to the doubt. In Avicenna's view, motion through the middle of the path of a heavenly body is one, simple, and everlasting. This unity is stronger than the unity the doubters reject. Such motion depends on the one, simple, unchanging Creator, while its changing parts depend on changing events. This is how the changing is linked to the eternal.

The argument is stronger if based on this: each part of a motion is actual in relation to the part before it and potential in relation to the part after it. The same part cannot be absent between its potential and its actuality. Our senses—sight especially—often mislead us about motion and rest.
This means the resistance that opposes forced motion, unlike the resistance of the medium in natural motion. A body thrown upward through air or water also meets resistance from the medium.

You may ask: how can speed and slowness be understood independently of each other when their definitions mention less time and more time, which involve a comparison? I reply, first, that these expressions need not be accepted as definitions. Second, the discussion concerns speed and slowness in themselves; here “less” and “more” can simply mean a small or large amount. We can also speak of one motion as faster than or slower than another, but those are relative descriptions.

The distinction is like one made earlier about length: length in itself need not be longer or shorter than anything, though comparative length is relative. Number can be many without comparison, while being more numerous than another number is a relative property.

If true opposites must differ as greatly as possible, speed and slowness do not seem to be opposites: for any fast or slow motion, we can imagine one faster or slower still. The proposed limits of moving and resisting powers do not resolve this. Opposition depends on what things are by nature, not on which examples happen to exist.

In truth, what belongs to every motion is its speed, understood as its way of passing and coming to an end. When we compare motions, we describe one as faster or slower than another. The same motion is slower than one motion and faster than a different one. These are relations, not two qualities opposed in themselves. Just as existence can be described as stronger or weaker by comparison, speed admits similar comparisons. Speed belongs to motion itself even though we divide motions into fast and slow; likewise unity belongs to existence even though we distinguish one and many.

The slower motion has more composition, just as multiplicity comes from a more complex existence. The simpler the motion, the faster it is; greater complexity makes it slower. I know of no leading philosopher who has put this conclusion in these words, but the arguments leave no way around it. Consider it carefully.
Time is included in the definitions of speed and slowness. This is why motion can be divided into faster and slower forms by time, as well as by the other things on which it depends.

This is like the relation between existence and what a thing is. Without a particular existence, we could not draw out what the thing is; in that sense, what it is depends on existence. In thought, we can treat what a thing is as the subject and existence as what is said of it, but in the world they are one. The commentator's own answer is that motion beyond time causes time, while motions within time depend on particular times. This fits Sadra's view that nature is always changing, and that time measures this renewal.
For example, heat and cold can each be agents in a process of becoming black.

“Beginning” and “end” here do not mean rest at the start and finish. They mean the connected states through which motion passes. Motion is a flowing state, understood by its relation to what comes before and after; as Sadra says, its nature is to leave and to aim.

A line is simple in a way a body is not. A body can keep its matter while its form changes. Straightness and curvature either define a line or belong to two kinds of line; either way, changing between them means the line itself changes.
This is another way to deny that straight and circular motions oppose each other: straight and circular paths are not opposites, as the previous chapter explained.
That is, the point a straight motion begins from would be the point a circular motion moves toward, so the two motions would run in opposite directions.
The author says “motions along them” rather than “motion along the chord,” so the point applies to every circular path compared with other circular paths.
If the arcs were all one kind, they would share one definition. But their essential features differ, so their kinds differ too.

The commentator distinguishes the celestial body's position at the end of one day's motion from its position at the start of the next. He questions the claim that these are the very same point in circular motion. The passage first denies that circular motions oppose each other, then signals a more careful account.

The reply misses its target: it assumes a shared endpoint, though none has been shown. If there were an actual shared boundary, it would be a point between lines, an instant between times, or rest between motions. In that case, the boundary would divide the lines, times, or motions into two. The critic's deeper point is sound: opposite motions are two individual motions of different kinds. If they joined without rest into one continuous motion, they would be one individual motion despite belonging to different kinds, which is impossible.

The commentator clarifies that the argument uses “becoming black” for the movement that follows reaching the darkest point and turns toward white. That movement does not begin while the thing is still white. A white thing may have a remote possibility of becoming white again, but that does not prove the same power is producing both changes at once.

The proof uses an inward tendency in the body. It can begin at an instant and can be felt as the body resists what blocks it. This avoids the earlier problem about motion having no first part: separation takes time, though it has a boundary instant.
This is not a special exception added to the proof. Turning back means leaving the destination of the first motion altogether; passing a point along the path is not the same thing.
The source word here means the felt tendency by which a body resists what blocks it. It does not mean desire or love, which the commentator says runs through all things.

The ball's motion in this example comes only from its connection to the turning wheel, not from itself. The argument concerns motion a thing has in itself; carried motion is like rest when considered on its own.

The objector is not agreeing that the stone rests. The point is that rest would not occur because the force blocking it had been removed; the force is still there, and no cause of rest has yet been shown.

Motion shows that the unusual force is present. If air resistance exists only while the stone is moving, it cannot explain how that force disappears: its supposed cause of removal depends on the very motion that reveals the force.
Once the critic has asked what causes the unusual force to disappear, he asks what causes the stone to rest above.

The question is not why the obstacle is missing after the resistance ends. The point is that Avicenna claims an extra power is needed to make the stone rest, though a balance of powers should already explain rest. The claim that this balance must last is weak: bodily powers have limited effects, especially forced powers, which do not act forever or most of the time.

“Condition” is intended here, not “preparatory cause.” A condition remains with what depends on it; a preparatory cause can act earlier. The weakening and its cause prepare for rest, while balance is a condition.
Nature resists forced movement, just as a living body resists illness and tends toward recovery and its natural activity.
The air's impacts prepare the body for rest and weaken the unusual force. A preparatory cause does not need to be present at the moment its result occurs. Nature itself is the direct cause of rest.

Someone who denies rest between motions will not accept rest at the final instant of the first motion. They accept it only after the return or turn has been completed. The proof needs rest at the upper point.
The commentator explains that an absence can still need a cause. Rest may be a possible absence, or it may follow from a positive state; either way, a cause is involved.
The eight heavenly spheres move by following the outermost sphere. Their motion is neither in themselves nor forced, since nothing forces the heavens.
Carried motion is still connected to one of the three main kinds. The heavenly spheres move by following the outermost sphere; a passenger on a ship is carried along while at rest in themselves.

The pulse should not be called voluntary, even if breathing can be controlled in some ways. The heart and arteries pulse several times during each expansion and contraction of the breathing organs, and are refreshed by what comes from the chest and lungs.

The claim that the pulse is movement from place to place is weak, since it does not change location. Unless it means a tightening motion, the pulse is better understood as a change in size: expansion and contraction, with rest between them. If it were a change of position, it would resemble a person gradually lying down and standing up, passing through countless positions with a pause between movements. The note means that “most doctors” refers to less careful medical writers, who usually classified the pulse as a change of position or size, not movement from place to place.

The passage appears to combine different views about the pulse. One holds that the heart and arteries contract and expand through their own nature. Another holds that the movement comes from the living power in the heart, as discussed earlier. A third places that power in the arteries. I have recorded other views in my poem Gems of Insight. Perhaps saying that the heart and arteries produce the movement simply means that they receive it. — س ره

The pulse, breathing, and growth in animals are examples of motion directed by the soul through nature. This is why the author adds a fifth kind of motion, alongside the four already listed. Celestial motion is also placed in this fifth kind.

These explanations avoid two misunderstandings: that the heavens' form is a nature like the four elements, and that their motion is natural in exactly the same way as the elements' motion. Both explanations say that celestial motion is chosen, but resembles natural motion because it follows one steady pattern.
That is, “nature” is being used in one of its several meanings described earlier.

This is the view of Thābit ibn Qurra. He says the earth is not held at the center because the heavens push or pull it. Those are two other explanations. The higher does not pay attention to the lower.

We could also choose the first answer: the earth seeks the center in the sense that it seeks to have its own center coincide with the center of the world. It does not seek to occupy a point at the center. As for the earth's parts, no part exists on its own until something separates it. Until then, the earth is one continuous body. A part separated by force joins the whole again when the force is removed, so it is not an independent thing whose aim we can judge by itself. But the view that heavy bodies seek the center and light bodies seek the outer edge—even with the meaning we have given it—would mean that water and air are always being forced out of their natural places. The better answer, as the author says, is that water's natural region is around the earth, while fire's is inside the outermost sphere. Then neither needs to be constantly forced from its natural place. Someone may object that if this is so, water should not move toward the center when we dig down toward it, and air should not rise toward the outer edge if there is no fire in its way. But both move that way to prevent empty space. Their contact with air in these cases is forced, and they flee from it, as in the hanging-brick example discussed below.

Someone might say that empty space could be avoided by more air flowing in. I reply that all things naturally resist empty space. Air and oil enter the space left by a burning wick. Blood, flesh, and other matter rise into the space inside a cupping glass. This is a natural aversion to emptiness, not a choice made after thought that can be set aside when something else acts. When a flame rises from the wick, the oil follows so that no empty space forms, even if another flame or air is already there. In the same way, when a cupper draws out the air, blood and flesh rise into the space inside the glass.
You may say that a body already has a natural straight tendency. But my point is that it can also receive forced circular motion, and so it may have a natural circular motion too.

The kind of jagged form remains, but not the same individual jagged form. If the individual form lasted, the body would have to remain forced forever. Particular jagged forms, such as those of mountains, do not last through earthquakes or the breaking that comes from severe cold. They are changed and come to the “gate of gates,” since the flow of existence never stops. This is one way to understand the verse, “You see the mountains, thinking them fixed, while they pass like clouds” (Qur'an 27:88).

Nature resists the body's forced state and keeps turning toward its natural goal. The outside condition is temporary and goes away. Natural tendency, by contrast, belongs to the body itself and is strong; impacts from the air do not remove it.

If the stone only received an upward tendency, without any change in its specific form, there would be no likeness between the effect and its source. The problem goes away if the body's substance changes continuously, in a weakened or partial way, as Sadra says.

Iron and fire each have a broad range of forms. Sadra does not mean that they are made by combining two separate forms. Rather, the iron's form lies between the two. You could call it an iron form, and you could also call it a fire form. This resembles a mixture of hot and cold, dry and moist. The form that produces the mixture remains in a middle state, not in a pure state. This all follows from the theory of substantial motion: the change here is not only in qualities, such as tendencies that come upon a body. The body's very nature also changes.

The matter has already been fully shaped and made into a stone by the stony form. The form that makes it light then belongs to a subject that already has its own form. In that way, the lightening form is an accident.

This passage can be read in two ways. First, the outside force gives the body an unusual, forced tendency that lasts until the motion ends. Avicenna is reported to hold this view. Calling an accident a “power” is not unusual, as we saw in the discussion of power and action. Second, the cause that lasts until the motion ends may be nature. The outside force gives it this role by changing nature into an unusual state or by creating a form that makes the body light. On this second reading, there are five possible views, not four. When Sadra says that one sound view remains, he means the second reading. He does not discuss the first separately because it leads back to the view he has already explained.
Sadra first mentioned number, size, and time. Here he speaks only of number and time because a power's effects are actions and motions, and a motion has no fixed spatial size. Its measure is time.

A difference in strength results from a difference in duration. There is no problem in treating the cause and its effect as two kinds of difference. In this passage, “duration” is set against an increase in duration. The author takes the rest of this explanation from al-Tusi's commentary on The Pointers, where he discusses whether bodily powers have limits. He uses it here to show the difference between variation in time, in number, and in strength.

This applies to effects that are motions. If an effect is not motion and its source is not bodily, it may be unlimited. For example, divine power is unlimited in strength, as God is unlimited in light. His creative act lies beyond motion and time.

This concerns bodily powers that spread through a body and qualities that exist throughout it. They can increase or decrease just as a quantity can. They are unlike powers and qualities that do not depend on bodies. A length, for example, can keep getting smaller without reaching a final smallest length; whiteness can do the same. The same applies to whether two quantities can be measured by a common unit. If one amount is greater than another, we can keep subtracting the smaller from the larger without reaching a final point. Quantity can be divided without end, unlike number, which ends at one.
This means weakness, decrease, and increase in strength. As we have already seen, a bodily power cannot be infinitely strong.

The proof can be summarized this way. If a body had no natural tendency, it would not move. We know from experience that this conclusion is false. The link in the proof is this: if the body moved without a tendency, its motion would either take time or not. If it took time, the three examples would force the time to match that of a body with a tendency. If it did not take time, it would lack one of the six things that motion must have. So motion without a natural tendency is impossible, and every body must have such a tendency.
The claim is a conditional: “If this motion occurred, it would take time.” Saying that the conditional is true does not mean that the motion actually occurs.

Someone may say that equal times do not follow from the assumptions. I reply that saying a motion without any tendency would take time is like saying, “If an immaterial being moved, its motion would take time.” This does not mean that a real motion has one amount of time for the movement itself and another for its speed, slowness, or resistance. Motion and speed exist together, just as a general kind and its specific form exist together. If two motions agree in one of the three measures discussed above but differ in another, the third must differ by the same ratio.

This is the natural tendency within the body that resists the tendency imposed by the outside force. The body's natural tendency and the outside force are held constant in the examples, while the three motions differ. So the differing motions cannot all come from the same unchanged cause; their tendencies must differ too.

On this reading, there is no need to use all three motions in the proof. A shorter argument is enough: if forced motion had no inner resistance, there would be no speed or slowness. Without speed or slowness, there would be no motion. So forced motion would not exist, which is false.

The same point applies to motion from the soul. Even if the soul's imagination and choice were at their strongest, they would not necessarily produce the same motion in all three examples. If someone says this also applies to an outside force at its strongest, “outside force” here does not mean an agent acting by choice. It means a force that acts by nature. A natural force always acts in the same way.

Al-Tusi is setting out a general point, apart from how it is used in this particular proof. His point is sound. The objector's quick response is unfair. If neither nature nor the outside force varies, but the motions do vary, then there must be some resistance that accounts for the difference. This is the result the objector wanted.

Someone may ask what sets the strength of the tendency if nature itself does not vary. The best answer is the one given by the author. A tendency is a quality that can be stronger or weaker. It lies between nature and motion: it connects the changing motion to the stable nature. It varies in itself, and outside causes help produce it.

The point is about tendency. Even when there is only one inside or outside resistance, motion can still have different degrees of speed and slowness. So the three motions in the proof cannot be set by the same resistance while their speeds differ. The same issue would arise if someone argued against empty space by using only the inside tendency, and left out resistance from the medium.

The argument can be made more briefly: if anything in the world moves by force, then nature exists. Forced motion goes against nature, so it cannot happen where there is no nature. The cause of forced motion is always a bodily power with a position. It acts by pulling or pushing, or by preparing a body to become hot, cold, or something else. A body can receive such an effect only if it already has a particular nature. Matter by itself cannot receive it until it has a definite substance and belongs to a kind. In the stages of an embryo's growth, for example, the elements prepare matter for the form of semen, and the semen prepares it for the form of the embryo. Forms do not oppose each other, and one specific form does not turn into another. Sadra points to this principle here. He could have made a shorter argument from it, though changing the proof in the middle of a reply may be poor form in a debate. If he is pointing to a different proof, however, the change is acceptable.

Sadra is answering a possible doubt: someone may be surprised that such a long argument is needed to prove both that bodies have powers and natures and that empty space is impossible. He says there are many ways to prove these claims. Some were given earlier, some here, and one short proof can be drawn from his argument: if there is forced motion in the world, there must be a natural tendency, because forced motion goes against nature. Another proof was given above: if there were no tendency, motion would have to remove itself as soon as it began.
In other words, without nature there would be no motion, since a separate, immaterial cause is too exalted to produce motion directly.

A specific form, which is called “nature” in simple bodies, makes a body the kind of thing it is. A body is a real kind in the wider order of things, but it is not a complete kind of thing among bodies until it has a specific form. Matter may already have a bodily form, but it still needs a specific form to become a particular kind of body. That form is the source of the body's different effects and the starting point of its motion and tendency. In this sense, it is called nature: the first source of a body's own motion and rest.
The phrase “within them” means that these powers are spread throughout bodies and divided with them. They do not merely sit on the surface.

This rules out the view that God directly produces these motions without powers or natures acting between Him and bodies. It also addresses the problem of how a changing effect can be connected to an unchanging cause.
